note: The second stories of php2shell, as signals. The first story counts attacks. The second asks who was exposed and was not hit, who was hit and what that says about them, and what was within reach behind the server. This page is the site's analysis, built from captured sources: each layer, signal and barrier cites the evidence it rests on, and says plainly where there is none.

families.name: Exploitation signals
families.question: Who is trying, at what scale, and does anything land?
families.now: Attempts at scale from the parties positioned to see them; one honeypot hit four days before release; both CVEs in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since 26 October, with no victim named; no confirmed compromise.
families.watch: A named victim; what CISA's updated PHP alert says of its evidence; a gap between the date a site was compromised and the date it says so.

families.name: Patching signals
families.question: How fast does the fix reach the servers, and who is left behind?
families.now: Releases for 8.2 to 8.5 within the hour, distributions recorded fixed in the NCSC-NL inventory from 15:30 UTC on 21 October, and a long tail: 440 of 724 inventory rows still under investigation at 15:28 UTC on 22 October, about 25 hours after release, and 1.57 million unpatched hosts on the first day.
families.watch: Censys or VulnCheck recounting unpatched hosts; the inventory's investigation rows resolving; the end-of-life tail.

families.name: Network protection signals
families.question: What stood in front of the server, and did it hold?
families.now: Edge rules live from 03:02 UTC on 21 October at Cloudflare and the same day at Akamai, Fastly and Imperva; Cloudflare saw attackers mutating payloads to get past them; Fortinet's signatures ship in alert-only mode. Some of the devices in front of servers run PHP themselves: Palo Alto lists every PAN-OS and Panorama version as affected, and the inventory has Check Point's firewall web interfaces and NetScaler ADC as vulnerable.
families.watch: A vendor reporting a bypass of its rule; a security appliance compromised through its own PHP.

families.name: Internal vulnerability signals
families.question: Once code runs as the web worker, what can it reach?
families.now: No captured source describes what was behind a compromised server, because no compromise is confirmed. What exists are the signals defenders were told to look for: a PHP worker spawning a shell or downloading tools, new outbound connections from workers, and the warning that a clean log proves little.
families.watch: The first incident report that says what the attacker reached: credentials on the host, the database, the internal network, a cloud role.

barriers.what: Edge rules at the big WAF providers
barriers.at_note: Cloudflare, about nine hours before disclosure by its own account; Akamai, Fastly and Imperva the same day
barriers.gap: No edge protection, or rules not switched on

barriers.what: The first official advice to be ready to take systems offline
barriers.at_note: the NSA on X, before the CVE records were published
barriers.gap: No way to pull a system quickly, or nobody with the authority to decide

barriers.what: Fixed PHP releases for every supported branch
barriers.at_note: tags at 13:35 UTC; the advisory at 14:00
barriers.gap: No patch pipeline: the organisation could not rebuild and redeploy PHP in time, or did not know where it ran

barriers.what: Configuration mitigations for those who could not patch
barriers.gap: No configuration management: settings could not be pushed to every server

barriers.what: Fixed packages from the operating systems
barriers.at_note: the first one recorded in the NCSC-NL inventory (Red Hat); Ubuntu, Debian and the Docker image by 16:03
barriers.gap: Routine updates not applied, or the server on a distribution nobody maintains

barriers.what: Host and log signals to look for
barriers.at_note: CISA's alert, dated 21 October with no time; community Sigma, Suricata and Falco rules followed
barriers.gap: No monitoring that would see a worker spawn a shell or call out

barriers.what: Defence in depth behind the worker
barriers.at_note: not a release: either it was built before 21 October or it was not there
barriers.gap: Credentials the worker can use, a database it can read, an internal network it can call: the reach that turns code execution into a breach

reading: A site that was exposed and not exploited is evidence too. Attempts ran in the millions and confirmed compromises stayed at zero; the difference is the population this page is about, and nobody has counted it.

Code execution as the web worker is reach, not yet a breach. Whether it becomes one depends on what that worker can open: the newsroom's question about any secret, 'can the attacker reach the system it opens?', asked of a whole server.

Every barrier has a time. A compromise after a barrier was available says something about the organisation, not only about the bug: after 03:02 UTC on 21 October, that there was no edge protection in front; after 14:00, that there was no pipeline to patch; and at any time, if the attacker reached anything that mattered, that there was nothing behind the worker.
